opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think robotics today is a bit where NLP was maybe five or six years ago. The big bottleneck is data. In language, we had the whole internet: billions of web pages people had written for decades, just sitting there waiting to be trained on. In robotics, there's nothing like that. Every lab collects its own data, on its own robot, in its own format, with its own camera setup. Then it mostly stays on a hard drive somewhere. So you have hundreds of groups each sitting on a small island of data, and nobody can really build on top of each other.

What the Hub can do, and what we've been trying to do with LeRobot, is first agree on a common format. That sounds boring, but it's actually the most important thing. If your episodes, your joint states, your camera streams, and your actions are all stored the same way, then suddenly a dataset recorded in Paris on a cheap arm can be loaded with one line of code by a student in Tokyo or a startup in San Francisco. That's what happened with text and models: once things became easy to share, the community just exploded.

The second thing is scale through community. We're never going to have one company teleoperate enough robots to cover all the diversity of the real world: all the kitchens, all the objects, all the lighting conditions. But if you have thousands of people with low-cost robots, each recording a few hundred episodes and pushing them to the Hub, you very quickly get a long tail of diversity that no single lab could afford. We've already seen people do hackathons where in a weekend they collectively record more varied data than some published datasets.

And the third point is openness itself. When the data is open, you can inspect it, visualize it, see where it's bad, filter it, and improve it. You can benchmark fairly because everyone trains on the same thing. And you avoid a situation where only two or three very well-funded companies own all the robot data and therefore own the foundation models for robotics. For me that's really the goal: make sure that when the "GPT moment" for robotics happens, it happens in the open, and that it's built by everyone, not just a few.

There are still hard problems, of course. Different embodiments, different action spaces, data quality is very uneven, and how you mix simulation with real data. But you can only start solving those problems once the data is actually in one place where people can look at it together. So I think shared datasets are kind of the foundation for everything else.

r001.rationale: The response discusses people contributing robot episodes and teleoperation, but does not state that automating tasks requires recording a person or robot performing those tasks.

r002.rationale: It says diverse environments and conditions matter, but does not connect insufficient environmental diversity to poor generalization to new environments.

r003.rationale: It proposes that thousands of contributors upload episodes to the Hub, creating a long tail of environmental and situational diversity no single lab could afford.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the first thing to say is that robotics has a data problem that looks very different from what we saw in language. With text, the data already existed. The internet had been accumulating it for decades, and the challenge was mostly about scale and filtering. In robotics, the data doesn't exist yet. Every trajectory, every demonstration, every teleoperated episode has to be physically generated by someone moving a robot in the real world. That's slow and expensive, and it means most labs end up with tiny, siloed datasets collected on their own hardware in their own setup.

That fragmentation is really the core problem. You'd have one group with a few hundred episodes of a Franka arm stacking cubes, another with a few thousand episodes of a mobile base opening doors, and none of it talks to each other. Different formats, different camera conventions, different ways of recording actions. So even if you wanted to pool it all together, you'd spend months just on data engineering before you trained anything.

What we've tried to do with the Hub, and especially with LeRobot, is attack that from a few angles. The first is just standardization. If there's a common format for recording episodes, with observations, actions, and metadata all stored consistently, then a dataset from one lab becomes immediately usable by another. That sounds boring, but it's probably the single biggest unlock. It's the same thing that happened with Transformers, where having a shared interface meant a model from Google could be fine-tuned by a student in a bedroom the same afternoon.

The second angle is aggregation. Once things are in a shared format on a shared platform, you can start building the robotics equivalent of a large pretraining corpus by stitching together hundreds of community datasets. Individually they're small, but collectively they start to cover a real diversity of embodiments, tasks, and environments. And diversity is what you need for generalization. A policy trained on one robot in one kitchen is a demo. A policy trained across many robots in many kitchens starts to be a foundation model.

The third angle is lowering the cost of contribution. The reason so few people generate robotics data is that the hardware has been expensive and the tooling has been painful. If you can bring the robot down to a few hundred dollars, make the teleoperation setup easy, and let someone push their episodes to the Hub with one command, then you unlock a much larger population of contributors. It's the open-source dynamic. Thousands of people each contributing a little ends up outpacing any single company's internal collection effort.

And then there's something more subtle, which is reproducibility and evaluation. Right now, robotics results are notoriously hard to compare because everyone evaluates on their own setup. If datasets and the models trained on them are both public, you at least get a shared starting point. People can see exactly what data a policy was trained on, retrain it, and compare honestly.

I don't want to oversell it. Shared datasets don't solve the sim-to-real gap, and they don't solve the fact that real-world data collection is still fundamentally bottlenecked by physical time. But they do solve the coordination problem, which is the one that's been holding the field back the most. The models are getting good enough. What's been missing is the data flywheel, and I think a shared, open hub is the only realistic way to build one.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics trajectories and demonstrations are physically generated by someone moving a robot, and discusses recording episodes for training.

r002.rationale: It says a policy trained across many robots and kitchens has the diversity needed for generalization, unlike one trained in a single kitchen.

r003.rationale: It proposes stitching together community datasets on a shared platform to cover a wider diversity of environments.

astra-6.text:
I think the big opportunity is to make it possible to build on each other’s data. In robotics, collecting data is expensive: you need a robot interacting with the physical world, and each team may have a different robot, different sensors, and a different way of recording what happens. So even when people share data, combining it can be difficult.

A shared hub can help by making those datasets discoverable and easier to use, with common formats and clear documentation about how they were collected. That lets a team start from existing demonstrations and then collect additional data for its particular robot or task, rather than collecting everything from scratch.

But hosting the data is only part of it. An action on one robot doesn’t necessarily mean the same thing on another. You still need to work on how to represent those differences and learn across them. I think sharing datasets alongside the tools to inspect them, the models trained on them, and the evaluations is what makes this really useful. It gives the community a way to figure out together which data actually helps robots generalize.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics data collection requires a robot interacting with the physical world and mentions existing demonstrations, but it does not state that training requires recording a person or robot performing the task.

r002.rationale: It discusses differences among robots, sensors, and recording methods, but does not identify insufficient environmental diversity as a cause of poor generalization to new environments.

r003.rationale: The response proposes sharing datasets from different teams through a hub, but does not say that pooling them would increase environmental diversity in robotics training data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the big challenges in robotics is that the data is very fragmented. Different teams have different robots, different sensors, different ways of recording actions. So even when people share data, it can be quite difficult for someone else to use it.

The opportunity with the Hub is to make these datasets easier to discover, understand, and combine. You need the recordings, but you also need the context: What robot was used? What does an action represent? How was the task performed? Having common formats and good documentation can make a big difference.

Then you can start pooling experience across teams, across environments, and potentially across different robots. That doesn’t mean data from one robot will automatically transfer to another—that’s still a research challenge. But it gives the community a much stronger foundation for studying that transfer, instead of everyone having to collect everything from scratch.

r001.rationale: It mentions recordings and recorded actions, but does not state that training robots to automate tasks requires recording a person or robot performing those tasks.

r002.rationale: It notes that pooling data across environments could help study transfer, but does not identify insufficient environmental diversity as a cause of poor generalization to new environments.

r003.rationale: It says the Hub can help teams discover and combine datasets, then pool experience across environments, clearly conveying that contributor datasets could broaden environmental diversity.
